proposed_features.description: Higher education levels (Bachelors, Prof-school) are strongly correlated with higher income brackets, while HS-grad is more common in lower brackets.
Professional and managerial roles typically command higher salaries than sales, service, or other roles.
Government and self-employment sectors often have different pay structures compared to private sector employment, with government roles often being higher paid for similar education.
Non-zero capital gains are a direct indicator of investment income, which is a strong predictor of higher total income.
Working significantly more than 40 hours often correlates with higher income, while part-time work (<35) often correlates with lower income.
Married individuals often have higher household incomes or are in more stable, higher-paying positions compared to separated or never-married individuals.
Income generally peaks in middle age (35-50). Younger individuals (<25) and older individuals may have lower incomes due to experience or retirement.
Certain combinations of sex and occupation have known wage gaps or specific pay scales that influence the income bracket.
While all examples are US, in broader datasets, native country can indicate visa status or local wage scales, though here it acts as a baseline constant.
Being a 'Husband' or 'Wife' often correlates with being the primary earner in a household, potentially influencing reported income levels compared to 'Not-in-family' or 'Own-child'.
While sensitive, demographic data often correlates with income distribution patterns in historical datasets, serving as a proxy for socioeconomic background.
The final weight (fnlwgt) can sometimes correlate with the representativeness of the record; very low or very high weights might indicate specific sampling strata, though this is a weak feature.
Presence of capital losses might indicate active trading or financial management, which can be associated with higher income levels, though often co-occurs with gains.

The match between education level and occupation (e.g., Prof-school with Prof-specialty) indicates a high-value skill set, whereas mismatch (e.g., Bachelors with Other-service) might indicate lower income.
